clinicalPearls: Presents typically as limbic encephalitis with prominent, sometimes disproportionate, psychiatric and behavioural disturbance alongside memory loss.
Middle-aged women are most often affected, distinguishing its demographic from the older male predominance of LGI1 and CASPR2.
A high proportion of cases are paraneoplastic, linked to thymoma, lung, breast and ovarian tumours, so systematic tumour screening is essential.
The antibody targets subunits of the AMPA glutamate receptor and causes receptor internalisation, reducing excitatory synaptic transmission.
Isolated psychiatric presentations can lead to initial misdiagnosis as a primary psychiatric disorder.
Relapses are relatively frequent, so surveillance and maintenance immunotherapy are often required.
Coexisting neuronal or onconeural antibodies may accompany AMPA receptor antibodies and broaden the phenotype.
Seizures and confusion commonly occur, but the psychiatric prominence and tumour association are key clues.
reference.pathophysiology: AMPA (alpha-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid) receptors are ionotropic glutamate receptors composed of GluA1-GluA4 subunits that mediate the majority of fast excitatory synaptic transmission and are pivotal to synaptic plasticity and memory in the hippocampus. Pathogenic IgG antibodies, chiefly directed against the GluA1 and GluA2 subunits, bind the extracellular domain and drive cross-linking and internalisation of surface AMPA receptors, reducing receptor density at excitatory synapses. This depletion impairs synaptic transmission and plasticity in limbic circuits, producing amnesia, seizures and neuropsychiatric disturbance; unlike some other syndromes the antibody effect is a titre-dependent, largely reversible reduction in receptor number rather than fixed structural damage, which underlies potential recovery with immunotherapy and the tendency to relapse if antibody production resumes. A strong paraneoplastic component, with tumours of the thymus, lung, breast and ovary expressing AMPA-receptor antigens, frequently triggers the autoimmune response, so relapse or refractoriness should prompt renewed search for malignancy.
additionalDifferentials: Anti-LGI1 and other antibody-mediated limbic encephalitides
Primary psychiatric disorder such as an acute psychotic or affective episode
Paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis with onconeural antibodies
additionalInvestigations: Serum and cerebrospinal fluid cell-based assay for AMPA receptor (GluA1/GluA2) IgG
Whole-body cross-sectional imaging to screen for thymoma and lung, breast and ovarian tumours
Brain MRI for medial temporal involvement
Electroencephalography for seizures and encephalopathic changes
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis with oligoclonal bands and infection exclusion
Testing for coexisting neuronal and onconeural antibodies
redFlags: Acute severe psychiatric disturbance with cognitive decline suggesting an organic cause
Identification of an underlying tumour on screening
Reduced level of consciousness or status epilepticus
reference.prognosis: Many patients improve with immunotherapy and tumour treatment, but relapses are common and prognosis is influenced by the nature of any underlying malignancy. Residual cognitive or psychiatric deficits may persist, and maintenance immunotherapy is frequently needed.
pitfalls: Misattributing an isolated psychiatric presentation to a primary psychiatric illness and delaying testing
Insufficient or non-repeated tumour screening despite the high paraneoplastic rate
Failing to institute maintenance immunotherapy in a relapsing disorder
Overlooking coexisting antibodies that alter management and tumour risk
Assuming a single negative malignancy screen excludes an occult tumour
references: Autoimmune and paraneoplastic encephalitis consensus guidance
